summary:
FireFusion — Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Fire Observations

NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS instruments both detect active fires, but at different resolutions and with different detection patterns, which makes it hard to compare the two or build a single clear picture of fire activity over time.

FireFusion, built by Team VU_Surveyors for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, brings MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one interactive platform. For a chosen Area of Interest, users can view harmonized fire data through maps, a temporal activity calendar, detection clusters, and supporting evidence like Fire Radiative Power (FRP) — all in one place instead of switching between separate satellite feeds.

The platform is meant for researchers, emergency responders, and land managers who need to track fire activity and act on it, giving them a faster way to see where fires are occurring, how they’re developing, and how the two satellite records line up.
details:
FireFusion is an open-source Earth-observation platform built by Team VU_Surveyors for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It tackles a specific problem in long-term wildfire analysis: NASA’s MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) satellites detect fires at different resolutions, and that mismatch creates inconsistent fire counts that make historical comparisons unreliable.

The platform runs a five-stage harmonization pipeline — data acquisition, normalization, spatial-temporal clustering, cross-sensor calibration, and aggregation. It maps detections onto a standardized 5.5 km common grid, clusters them with DBSCAN, and calibrates across sensors using a Poisson Generalized Linear Model (GLM), which reduces resolution-related bias and produces more consistent fire activity records.

On top of this, FireFusion offers interactive hotspot maps, burning activity calendars, cluster evidence exploration, cross-sensor validation, and seasonal anomaly analysis, so users can see where fires occur, track how activity shifts over time, and check how MODIS and VIIRS detections line up against each other.

Data comes from NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS) and the NASA POWER API. The stack is Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Shadcn UI, Python, FastAPI, DuckDB, Bun, Turborepo, and Docker.

Most fire-mapping tools just display hotspots; FireFusion statistically reconciles two sensors with different resolutions before showing you anything, which is the harder and more useful problem. That’s aimed at researchers and environmental professionals who need fire records they can actually trust across years and across instruments.
